title: Smart Salary Car: Convert Hourly to Annual Pay Under the National Minimum Wage or an Award
description: Use the smart salary car approach to convert your hourly rate to annual, fortnightly, and after-tax pay. Compare the National Minimum Wage with award rates, casual loading, and sup
salarySummary: For a full‑time employee on the National Minimum Wage ($26.44/hr), working 38 hours a week, the annual gross pay is about $52,250.

faqs.q: How do I convert an hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For a standard full‑time role, assume 38 hours per week. For example, $30 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $59,280 per year. This is a gross estimate; your actual take‑home pay will be lower after tax and Medicare, and super is paid on top.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and an award rate?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage ($26.44/hr from 1 July 2026) applies to employees not covered by an award or agreement. Award rates are set by the Fair Work Commission for specific industries and occupations, and they are often higher. You can find the correct minimum rate for your job using the pay guides from the Fair Work Ombudsman.

faqs.q: Does my hourly rate include casual loading and super?
faqs.a: Usually no. Casual loading (25% on top of the base rate) is added separately. Superannuation (12% of ordinary earnings from 1 July 2026) is paid on top of your gross wage, not included in the hourly rate. When using a calculator, enter the base hourly rate and tick the casual loading box if applicable. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Smart Salary Car: From Hourly to Annual Pay

Whether you are negotiating a new job, comparing a casual role with a permanent offer, or simply checking your pay, the **smart salary car** method helps you convert any hourly rate into an annual figure quickly. The basic formula is:

**Annual gross pay ≈ hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For a full‑time employee, we assume 38 hours per week – the standard ordinary hours under the National Employment Standards. If you work part‑time or irregular hours, adjust the weekly hours to match your usual schedule. The same formula works for a fortnight: multiply the weekly amount by 2.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the Fair Work Commission set the National Minimum Wage at **$26.44 per hour** ($1,004.90 per week for 38 hours). This is the legal floor for award‑free employees. However, most workers are covered by a modern award, which often has higher minimum rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes pay guides for each award, listing the correct classification rates, allowances, and penalty rates.

Using the smart salary car, a full‑time employee on the National Minimum Wage earns about **$52,250 annually** (before tax). But if you are covered by an award, your rate could be $28, $30, or more per hour. Always check the applicable award before relying on the national minimum.

### Casual Loading and Superannuation

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. For the National Minimum Wage, that means **$33.05 per hour** ($26.44 × 1.25). When using the [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) calculator, enter the base rate and tick the loading box – never type a rate that already includes the loading.

Superannuation is paid on top of your gross earnings. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee is **12% of ordinary earnings**, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For a full‑time worker on $52,250, the employer would contribute an extra $6,270 into your super fund. This is not part of your take‑home pay but is a valuable benefit.

### Tax and Take‑Home Pay

Your annual gross pay is not what lands in your bank account. The Australian Taxation Office applies the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (with possible reductions for low incomes). For a single person earning $52,250, the estimated tax is about $6,858 and Medicare $1,045, leaving a take‑home pay of roughly **$44,347 per year** – or about **$853 per week**.

To see your own figures, use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) estimator. Remember that HELP repayments, Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not included in this simple calculation.

### Why the Smart Salary Car Matters

The smart salary car approach gives you a clear, consistent way to compare job offers. A $35‑per‑hour casual role might look attractive, but after accounting for unpaid leave and no sick pay, a permanent $30‑per‑hour role with super and leave entitlements could be better value. Always consider the total package: base rate, loading, super, leave, and penalties.

For a quick reference, the [average pay](/topics/average-pay) in Australia (full‑time adult ordinary time) was $2,083.70 per week in May 2026, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. That translates to about $108,352 annually for a 38‑hour week – well above the national minimum.

### Using the Timesheet Calculator

Our [timesheet](/) tool lets you enter your base hourly rate and toggle casual loading. It shows your weekly, fortnightly, monthly, and annual gross pay, plus an estimate of tax and super. No need to memorise formulas – just type your rate and see the smart salary car in action.

Remember: annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax‑free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For award‑specific rates, always refer to the [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman. The smart salary car is your starting point – not the final word.
